title: CFD and ROM Analysis of Shell-And-Tube Units for Waste Management of Syngas Streams by Selective Mass Transfer
content: Palladium and its alloys are known to enable selective diﬀusion of hydrogen. This work builds on this property and presents a computational fluid dynamics (CFD) study for the design of a palladium-based hydrogen separation unit taking the form of a baﬄed shell-and-tube mass exchanger. The goal is to maximize the separated blue hydrogen from a shifted syngas. This separation has two beneﬁts: First, the separated hydrogen can be used as a fuel. Second, the remaining concentrated carbon dioxide can be either stored rather than emitted into the atmosphere or sold commercially. The selective diﬀusion is modeled macroscopically using Sieverts’ law with an Arrhenius-type expression for the permeability. The driving force is the diﬀerence of the square root of hydrogen’s partial pressure between the retentate stream (higher value) and the permeate stream (lower value). We also apply reduced-order modeling (ROM) to explore the off-design operating points for the dehydrogenation module. The results suggest that large improvements in the hydrogen separation from syngas that justify the incurred pressure drop are viable in two cases, which share in common the aim of intensifying the driving force: One case is when turbulators are introduced in the permeate stream to mitigate the steep gradient of the hydrogen concentration near the membrane, while the other case is when a series of separation units are used, and a hydrogen-free sweep gas is re-introduced at each unit. This study presents applied research in the field of waste management and sustainable technology, which has environmental gains by reducing atmospheric emissions.
